sections.overview: The common frog is widespread across Europe and divides its life between water and land. Its cycle links ponds, where eggs and larvae develop, with damp terrestrial places where adults feed and shelter. Adults exchange gases through both their lungs and moist skin; this allows some gas exchange underwater, while powerful hind limbs propel jumps and swimming.
sections.identification: Adults are compact frogs with smooth, damp skin and a dark patch behind the eye covering the eardrum. Their hind legs are moderately long and robust, unlike the agile frog Rana dalmatina, whose legs are very long and slender; exceptions occur, so use several traits together. Colour and markings vary widely, from brown and olive to grey, reddish, yellowish or greenish; colour alone is not enough for identification. In Britain, reported adult lengths reach about 9 cm in males and 13 cm in females, which are generally larger; these are upper figures, not typical sizes everywhere. Where similar brown frogs co-occur, combine several cues, including the eye patch, leg pattern, call and local range, rather than relying on one universal mark. A comparable, reliable adult body-mass range was not found in the consulted sources; body mass varies with sex, season and condition.
sections.habitat: Across its range, the species uses cool or damp landscapes, from woodland edges, grassland and moor to gardens and farmland. Adults may travel away from water after breeding, so a pond is only one part of their habitat: nearby cover and moist feeding grounds matter too. It breeds in shallow freshwater, including small ponds, lake margins, ditches and sometimes temporary puddles; local populations use the sites available in their landscape.
sections.diet: After metamorphosis, the frog hunts small invertebrates, including insects, slugs, snails and earthworms. It seizes suitable prey with its mouth and sticky tongue, then swallows it; prey size is limited by its mouth. Aquatic tadpoles feed differently: they scrape or gather algae and organic material from surfaces and pond sediment, with animal matter also recorded in some diets. Their feeding links fine detritus and plant growth to larger animals.
sections.behavior: The common frog is ectothermic: body temperature and metabolic pace depend strongly on surrounding conditions. It often forages at night or in damp weather, when its skin is less exposed to drying, and retreats beneath vegetation, stones or other cover. In cold seasons, activity and feeding fall and frogs overwinter in sheltered terrestrial sites or in water; refuges vary locally, and this species does not show the extreme freeze tolerance of some other frogs. At breeding ponds, males give a soft, repeated croak to attract mates and compete with nearby males.
sections.reproduction: Breeding dates shift with spring temperatures and local weather rather than following one universal calendar. In Britain, spawning can start in the southwest in January and is often seen from February onward elsewhere; these are regional examples. Males clasp females in amplexus; as the female releases eggs into water, the male releases sperm over them, so fertilisation is external. Each egg has its own gelatinous covering, and many eggs are laid together as a jelly mass floating just below the water surface. In British ponds, eggs hatch in about three weeks. Tadpoles then breathe underwater with gills. During metamorphosis, lungs develop and take part in air breathing as the gills regress; hind legs appear before forelegs, and the tail is gradually resorbed before froglets leave the water.
sections.ecology: Adult frogs and froglets are prey for herons, foxes, otters, snakes and other predators, while their aquatic eggs and tadpoles face fish, newts and insect larvae. The frog thus links terrestrial and pond food webs as both predator and prey.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment dates to 14 December 2008 and was published in 2009. It classified Rana temporaria as Least Concern with a stable trend, but the Red List record says this assessment needs updating; this historic result does not establish current status. Regional pressures include loss or degradation of breeding ponds and disease. In Britain, Natural England says garden ponds have partly offset the loss of traditional farm ponds. Protecting pond networks and nearby cover supports the full life cycle.
